import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 370

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/370](https://www.erdosproblems.com/370)
-/

namespace Erdos370

/--
Are there infinitely many $n$ such that the largest prime factor of $n$ is $< n^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and
the largest prime factor of $n + 1$ is $< (n + 1)^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

Steinerberger has pointed out this problem has a trivial solution.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos370.lean",
formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
"https://github.com/XC0R/formal-conjectures/blob/f58dea7d2cc5c9da2e050ec80a73e838b54a6dd2/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/370.lean#L73"]
theorem erdos_370 : answer(True) ↔
    { n | Nat.maxPrimeFac n < √n ∧ Nat.maxPrimeFac (n + 1) < √(n + 1) }.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos370

reformulations.difference: The cited external Lean proof's final theorem defines the greatest prime factor using `sSup {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ p ∣ n}`, whereas this file uses `Nat.maxPrimeFac`. These conventions differ at n = 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The definitions agree for n ≠ 1 by `Nat.maxPrimeFac_eq_sSup`. The exceptional candidate n = 1 fails the second inequality under either convention, since the greatest prime factor of 2 is 2 and 2 ≥ √2. Consequently the two candidate sets are equal, not merely equal up to finitely many exceptions. The external proof's reversed biconditional is handled by `iff_comm`. Both the set equality and the equivalence of the full statements were proved in /workspace/review/bridge.lean.

review.notes: The sole theorem faithfully states the source's infinitude question with both strict bounds. `answer(True)` and `research solved` agree with the source's “PROVED (LEAN)” affirmative status.
